content: The plant cuticle is a protective, waxy layer that is exclusively produced by the epidermal cells of leaves, young shoots, and other aerial plant organs that lack periderm. This cuticle is generally thicker on the upper surface of leaves. However, contrary to a common misconception, xerophytic plants in arid climates do not always have thicker cuticles than mesophytic plants in wetter climates. The cuticle is composed of an insoluble cuticular membrane that is both impregnated with and covered by soluble waxes. A key structural component of this membrane is cutin, a polyester polymer made up of inter-esterified straight-chain hydroxy acids that are cross-linked by ester and epoxide bonds. Additionally, the cuticle may contain a non-saponifiable hydrocarbon polymer known as cutan. The cuticular membrane is further impregnated with cuticular waxes and coated with epicuticular waxes, which are mixtures of hydrophobic aliphatic compounds and hydrocarbons, typically with chain lengths ranging from C16 to C36. The plant cuticle represents one of several evolutionary adaptations, alongside stomata, xylem, phloem, and intercellular spaces in stem and leaf mesophyll tissues, that plants developed over 450 million years ago during their transition from aquatic to terrestrial environments. These adaptations collectively enabled plant shoots to explore aerial environments while conserving water. This was achieved by internalizing gas exchange surfaces, enclosing them within a waterproof membrane, and incorporating a variable-aperture control mechanism—stomatal guard cells—that regulate the rates of transpiration and carbon dioxide exchange. Beyond its role as a barrier to water and molecular permeability, the microand nano-structure of the cuticle imparts specialized surface properties. These properties prevent external water, dirt, and microorganisms from contaminating plant tissues. Certain plants, such as the leaves of the sacred lotus (Nelumbo nucifera), exhibit ultra-hydrophobic and self-cleaning properties, a phenomenon described by Barthlott and Neinhuis in 1997 as the lotus effect. This effect has inspired potential applications in biomimetic technical materials. The waxy cuticle also serves a defensive function by forming a physical barrier that resists penetration by viral particles, bacterial cells, fungal spores, and growing fungal filaments.
